## Results

Between March 01, 2020, and Septembre 30, 2024, 385 individuals who committed sexual offenses against children have been screened for eligibility, of whom 16 have not been randomized (see @fig-diagram-consort-flowchart). 369 individuals were randomly assigned (182 placebo arm; 187 intervention arm). 213 participants have been included in the ITT sample (107 [57·2%] intervention arm; 106 [58·2%] placebo arm). 99 participants finished the WBI (44 [30·2%] intervention arm; 55 [22·4%] placebo arm). The trial was closed at Septembre 30, 2024. 70 participants were not able to finish the WBI before closing (39 \[59%\] intervention arm; 31 \[53%\] placebo arm).

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.no-count}

![Trial profile. ITT = Intention-to-treat population. StGB = German penalty law.](resources/figures/diagram_consort_flowchart.png){#fig-diagram-consort-flowchart}

:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

The MMRM for the cumulative time from baseline to finish module showed a significant treatment-by-time interaction across all timepoints (Module one: estimate 27, 95% CI 1·9 to 53, p = 0·035; Module two: estimate 44, 95% CI 3·3 to 85, p = 0·034; Module three: estimate 77, 95% CI 13 to 141, p = 0·019; Module four: estimate 113, 95% CI 30 to 195, p = 0·0078; Module five: estimate 126, 95% CI 30 to 223; p = 0·011; Module six: estimate 132, 95% CI 29 to 236; p = 0·013). Post-hoc pairwise comparisons showed longer cumulative completion times in the intervention arm for all modules. Unadjusted analyses indicated significant differences at module four (mean 260 days, SD 138, intervention arm; mean 223 days, SD 122, placebo arm; p = 0·048) and Module five (mean 325, SD 161 intervention arm; mean 258, SD 113 lacebo arm; p = 0·028), whereas differences at Modules one, two, three, and six did not reach significance (all p ≥ 0·053). After adjustment for multiple comparisons, none remained statistically significant (all q ≥ 0·17). Independent of treatment allocation, cumulative completion time increased substantially with each successive module (all p < 0·0001), rising from in the mean 69 days at module two (95% CI 55 to 83) to mean 333 days at module six (95% CI 273 to 393) compared with Module one (see apendix table XX for time required to complete each of the modules).

The MMRM for the time working on content revealed significant treatment effects at module one (estimate 360, 95% CI 49 to 671, p = 0.024) and at module 4 (estimate 236, 95% CI 19 to 453, p = 0.034), as well as at module 5 (estimate 324, 95% CI: 6.1 to 641, p = 0.046). No significant differences in time working on content were observed for module two (estimate 148, 95% CI -48 to 345, p = 0.14), module three (estimate 188, 95% CI -96 to 473, p = 0.19), or module six (estimate 93, 95% CI -142 to 328, p = 0.42). Post-hoc pairwise comparisons reveled no significant difference between trial arms (all p ≥ 0·18)

### Baseline characteristics

[@tbl-baseline-characteristics] shows sociodemographic, criminological and mental health baseline characteristics (see appendix pp. XXX). N = 2 of screened participants who have not been willing to take part in the trial gave informed consent to fill in the QNP, not allowing any inferences on the not participating population.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.no-count}

{{< include _includes/tbl_baseline_characteristics.qmd >}}

:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

Participants mean age was 41 years (range 20 to 68), predominantly male (216 [98%]; female: 2 [0·9%]; transsexual: 1 [0·5%]; other: 1 [0·5%]), and with a mean of 13 years of education (range 4 to 21 years). 144 [65%] participants were single, 44 [20%] married, 29 [13%] divorced and 4 widowed [1·8%]. With regard to strata, n = 89 (40%) participants were mixed offenders (at least one conviction §176 ff StG) and 132 (60%) were hands-off offenders (only convictions based on \$184b StGB). 176 (80%) participants were under community supervision (§§56, 57 StGB), 45 (20%) under post-release supervision (§§68ff StGB). 70 participants (32%) received an external in-face or medical treatment, 151 (68%) had no additional treatment. The court ordered treatment for 124 (56%), for 87 (44%) not. 48 (39%) of all participants, who had an court ordered treatment, received external treatment, 76 (61%) not. 180 participants (81%) had a low to medium static recidivism risk, 41 (19%) a medium to high static risk to re-offend at baseline. The most common psychiatric conditions were other depressive syndromes (20 [9%]), somatoform syndromes (17 \[7·7%\]), and major depressive syndromes (12 \[5·4%\]). Psychosocial functioning was generally good (130 [59%] reporting no difficulty at all). Seven (3·2%) participants full-filled the diagnostic criteria for a pedophilic disorder in the ICD-11 screener, 213 (97%) not. All participants had the German nationality. Data on ethnicity was not assessed.

### Main outcome

The mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) for the primary endpoint showed no evidence of a treatment effect over time, with no significant treatment-by-time interaction at any module (all p ≥ 0·15; see @tbl-prim-cares-mmrm). Covariables had no significant effect (all p ≥ 0·13).

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.no-count}

{{< include _includes/tbl_prim_CARES_mmrm.qmd >}}

:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

Sensitivity analysis revealed no different results (all p ≥ 0·169; see appendix table XX). An exploratory MMRM additionally adjusted for time since the beginning of module one yielded consistent results (all p ≥ 0·293; see appendix table X). The analysis of the IoD yielded consistent findings (all p ≥ 0·588; see appendix section “IoD”). Exploratory pairwise comparisons of change from baseline between treatment arms showed no differences between trial arms (all p ≥ 0·052; see appendix table X). 

Within‑arm pairwise comparisons showed a significant reduction from pre‑ to post at module one in the intervention arm (t = −2·85, p = 0·0050, Holm‑Bonferroni q = 0·030; estimated relative effect 0·451, 95% CI 0·417–0·485), with mean scores decreasing from 14 (SD 8) to 12 (SD 9). No significant changes were observed at later modules (all p ≥ 0·15; see appendix table X). In the placebo arm, a significant decrease from pre to post at module one (t = −3·88, p < 0·0001, q < 0·0001, p̂ = 0·428, 95% CI 0·392 to 0·465), with mean scores declining from 12 (SD 8) to 11 (SD 9) was observed. All other time-points showed significant effects (all p ≥ 0·54; see appendix table X).

### Secondary outcomes

[@tbl-sec-pairwise-intervention] shows descriptive statistics and the results of the pairwise comparisons for each secondary endpoint in the intervention arm, [@tbl-sec-pairwise-placebo] for the placebo arm. 

One endpoint showed statistically significant pre–post differences in the intervention arm. The ESIQ decreased from 90 (SD 12) to 87 (mean 12, p = 0·0010, q = 0·015), indicating a reduction in sexual interests in children. Three endpoints reached nominal significance but did not survive adjustment for multiple testing: the SSIC increased from mean 26·5 (SD 4·6) to 27·1 (4·3 p = 0·049, q = 0·59), the CVTRQ increased from mean 84 (SD 7) to 86 (SD 8) at post‑measurement indicating improved treatment readiness (p = 0·0060; Holm‑adjusted q = 0·078), and the DERS increased from mean 6·24 (SD 2·26) to 6·72 (2·25, p = 0·0050, q = 0·070). All other measures, including OQMPR, RCQ, F‑Soz‑U, BIS‑15, CUSI, NARQ, SPSI‑R, BMS, EKK‑R, and HBI‑19, showed no significant pre–post differences (all p ≥ 0·066). 

In the placebo arm, only one measure showed a statistically significant pre–post difference. The F‑Soz‑U increased from 3·74 (SD 0·84) at baseline to 3·88 (SD 0·89) at post‑measurement (p = 0·0030; Holm‑adjusted q = 0·045). All other measures, including CVTRQ, RCQ, OQMPR, UCLA, BIS‑15, CUSI, DERS, NARQ, SPSI‑R, BMS, ESIQ, SOI‑R, SSIC, EKK‑R, and HBI‑19, showed no significant pre–post differences (all p ≥ 0·12).

Exploratory analyses of change from baseline identified two questionnaires with statistically significant differences between the trial arms (table X). The ESIQ total score decreased in the intervention arm (mean change −3·6, SD 5·4), but remained largely unchanged in the placebo arm (mean change −0·1, SD 7·9, p = 0·0020, q = 0·030). Change from baseline in the DERS (impulsivity subscale) was greater in the intervention arm (mean change 0·49, SD 2·10) than in the placebo arm (mean change −0·15, SD 1·24), but reached not significance after correction for multiple comparisons (p = 0·024, q = 0·34). All other measures, including CVTRQ, RCQ, F‑Soz‑U, OQMPR, UCLA, BIS‑15, CUSI, NARQ, SPSI‑R, BMS, EKK‑R, SOI‑R, SSIC, and HBI‑19, showed no evidence of differences in cahnges from baseline between arms (all p ≥ 0·077; table X). Explorative regression models for secondary endpoints fitting strata as factors support this figure (see appendix Section "Secondary outcomes").

### Harms

During trial, no critical events were reported by SOs or STs; no events were reported to the sponsor or ethics committee. SOs excluded five (2.3%) participants due to recidivism (2 \[1.6%\] intervention arm; 3 \[2.7%\] placebo arm; see appendix table X). 

Preparation of contact with children, urges related to CSA, or urges related to CSEM were not reported. Two  participants (0·9%) reported planning of a contact with a child (1 [0·9%] intervention arm, 1 [0·9%] placebo arm). Two participant (1·9%) in the intervention arm reported high sexual tension, none in the placebo arm. One participant (0,9%) in the intervention arm reported losing control of sexual thoughts and activity, one in the placebo arm. Suicidal ideations were reported by two participants (1.9%) in the intervention arm, none in the placebo arm. Feeling unable to cope with mental burden was reported by nine (4·1%) participants (7 [6·5%] intervention arm; 2 [1·8%] placebo arm). A current mental crisis was reported by 15 (6·8%) participants (11 [10%] intervention arm; 4 [3·5%] placebo arm), and very poor current mood by 12 (5·4%) participants (8 [7·4%] intervention arm; 4 [3·5%] placebo arm). However, none of these differences were statistically significant (all p ≥ 0·065).

### Ancillary outcomes

The MMRM for the WHO‑5 showed no evidence for differences between trial arms over time, with no significant treatment-by-time interaction at any assessment (all p ≥ 0·11; table X). The estimated mean effects relative to placebo were 1·7 at module one, −1·8 at module two (pre), −1·6 at module two (post), −0·86 at module three (pre), −4·5 at module three (post), 0·10 at module four (pre), −4·3 at module four (post), −2·4 at module five (pre), −2·9 at module five (post), −1·9 at module six (pre), and −0·15 at module six (post). No significant effects were observed for co-variables (all p ≥ 0·24). Baseline scores were strongly associated with subsequent WHO‑5 outcomes (estimate 0·68, 95% CI 0·60 to 0·77, p < 0·0001). With respect to timepoint main effects, none of the modules differed significantly from module one (all p ≥ 0·24).

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.no-count}

{{< include _includes/tbl_sec_pairwise_intervention.qmd >}}

:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

The MMRM analysing the WAI‑SR COACH showed significant treatment-by-time interaction effects at several post‑module assessments (table X). Compared with placebo, estimates for the intervention arm were 2·4 at module one (95% CI 0·30 to 4·5, p = 0·025), 3·8 at module two (95% CI 1·2 to 6·5, p = 0·0044), 3·4 at module three (95% CI 0·96 to 5·9, p = 0·0067), and 4·3 at module five (95% CI 1·3 to 7·3, p = 0·0051). At module four, there was no significant effect (mean estimate 2·1, 95% CI -0·63 to 4·9, p = 0·13). No covariable shows a significant effect (all p ≥ 0·22). Pairwise pre–post comparisons within the intervention arm showed significant increases at module one, increasing from 42 (SD 11) to 44 (SD 9; p = 0·0020; q = 0·010), and at module five, increasing in the mean from 46 (SD 11) to 49 (SD 9; p = 0·0040, q = 0·016). No other modules in the intervention arm showed significant pre–post changes (all p ≥ 0·21). In the placebo arm, no significant pre–post changes were observed at any timepoint (all p ≥ 0·28; tables X). Exploratory analyses of change scores from baseline between treatment arms identified two timepoints with nominal differences, but not reaching significance after adjustment for multiple comparisons (table Z). Change from baseline at module one was greater in the intervention arm (median 3, Q1 −2 to Q3) than in the placebo arm (median 1, Q1 −3 to Q3 5, p = 0·025, q = 0·13). Similarly, change from baseline at module five was greater in the intervention arm (median 2, Q1 0 to Q3 6) than in the placebo arm (median 0, Q1 −2 to Q3 4, p = 0·036, q = 0·14). No other comparison showed evidence for differences between trial arms (all p ≥ 0·059).

Also the MMRM analysing the WAI‑SR SUPERVISOR showed significant treatment-by-time interaction effects at several post‑module assessments (table X). Compared with placebo, estimates for the intervention arm were 2·3 at module one (95% CI 0·64 to 4·1, p = 0·0073), 3·0 at module two (95% CI 0·87 to 5·2, p = 0·0061), 3·2 at module three (95% CI 1·2 to 5·3, p = 0·0022), and 3·6 at module five (95% CI 1·2 to 6·0, p = 0·0038). At module four, there was only a statistical trend (mean estimate 2·1, 95% CI -0·16 to 4·3, p = 0·068). No covariable shows a significant effect (all p ≥ 0·15). Pairwise pre–post comparisons within the intervention arm showed significant increases at module one, increasing from 43 (SD 9) to 46 (SD 8; p < 0·0001; q = < 0·0001); at module five significance after pairwise comparisons was not reached, increasing in the mean from 49 (SD 9) to 50 (SD 8; p = 0·046, q = 0·18), but significance after correction for pairwise comparisons was not reached at module five. No other modules in the intervention arm showed significant pre–post changes (all p ≥ 0·44). In the placebo arm, no significant pre–post changes were observed at any timepoint (all p ≥ 0·21). Exploratory analyses of change scores from baseline between treatment arms showed at module one a greater change from baseline in the intervention arm (median 4, Q1 −1 to Q3 6) than in the placebo arm (median 1, Q1 −3 to Q3 4, p = 0·0090, q = 0·045). Similarly, change from baseline at module five was greater in the intervention arm (median 1, Q1 0 to Q3 4) than in the placebo arm (median 0, Q1 −2 to Q3 2, p = 0·061, q = 0·24), but reached not significance after correction for multiple comparisons. No other comparison showed evidence for differences between trial arms (all p ≥ 0·40).
